extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (U.S. patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules for defending against a U.S. patent infringement action, including when specification defects, lack of novelty, prior use, or overbroad claims may be relied on and when a patent may be annulled or disclaimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirement for special matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant must give notice in writing to the plaintiff or his attorney thirty days before trial of certain special matters and may give the statute itself in evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute requires notice of 'certain special matters' and the giving in evidence of the statute; this is to guard the plaintiff against surprise. See also requirement to state names and residences of witnesses for prior use (footnote: no witness can be examined to prove prior use unless notice of his name and residence has been given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment or addition must be with intent to deceive to void patent
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification 'does not contain the whole truth' or 'contains more than is necessary' such concealment or addition must 'fully appear to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public' to justify declaring the patent void under the statute of 1836.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the act of 1836 the patent is not automatically void for defective specification; fraudulent intent (purpose to deceive the public) must be proved by the defendant to obtain vacatur of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable a skilled person to make and use the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make, compound, and use the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory prerequisite (§3). The purpose is to give the public the benefit of the invention after the monopoly expires; omission of material elements or insufficiency to enable a person of ordinary skill can be a defence to infringement (at common law made patent void; statute narrows relief to cases of fraudulent concealment for vacatur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain principle and several modes for machines
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of any machine the inventor 'shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes, in which he has contemplated the application of that principle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must not merely name parts but explain the principle and modes of application by which the invention is distinguished from others; this aids construction by skilled persons and delimiting the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what is new and what is old
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is an improvement on an existing machine, the patentee 'should distinguish what is new and what is old in his specification, so that it may clearly appear for what the patent is granted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification that mixes old and new without identifying the novel matter renders the patent broader than the invention and may make it void because it is impossible to tell what is claimed as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed novelty must appear with reasonable certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient if 'what is claimed as new appear with reasonable certainty on the face of the patent, either expressly or by necessary implication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the claimed new matter appears with reasonable certainty is a question of law on the construction of the patent and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defective specification can be a defense under general issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may show failure in any of the prerequisites on which authority to issue a patent depends under the general issue, without notice, to defend himself in the particular action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where the statute makes certain matters 'special defences' requiring notice to seek vacatur, failure of the prerequisites to issuance (e.g., sufficiency of specification) may be shown as a defence to defeat recovery in a single action without following the special-annulment procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent intent required only to annul the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of fraudulent intent is requisite only when the defendant seeks to have the patent declared void; it is not required merely to defeat the plaintiff's recovery in the particular action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant simply wishes to defend himself (obtain verdict in his favor), proof of defects need not show intent; but to secure a judgment that the patent is void the concealment or addition must be found to have been made to deceive the public (per Grant v. Raymond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites to issuing a patent are examinable in any suit
rubrics_metrics.description: The prerequisites (e.g., correct specification and description required by §3) to the issuance of a patent are examinable in any suit brought upon it, and failure in those prerequisites is a bar to recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the secretary's role is ministerial, courts may examine compliance with statutory prerequisites; failure to satisfy them can prevent enforcement of the patent irrespective of the patentee's intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of lack of novelty / prior knowledge or use
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence exists that 'the patentee was not the original and first inventor or discoverer of the thing patented, or of a substantial and material part thereof, claimed as new; or that it had been described in some public work, anterior to the supposed discovery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To rely on this defence the defendant must show prior knowledge, use, or description of the invention; such prior user or description may be proved by parol and the plaintiff's right relates back to the original discovery (though infringement must occur after patent date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict notice content for prior-use defense
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on prior use or prior possession to show lack of novelty the defendant 'shall state in his notice of special matter the names and places of residence of those whom he intends to prove to have possessed a prior knowledge of the thing, and where the same had been used.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision must be strictly complied with; the statute does not require notice of the time when such persons possessed the alleged knowledge and use. It is also to be inferred that notice should describe whether the whole or a part of the invention is charged with want of novelty, and in what public work it was described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proviso protecting good-faith patentee against foreign prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: If it satisfactorily appears that the patentee, at the time of application, believed himself to be the first inventor, the patent shall not be held void on account of the invention or any part having been before known or used in any foreign country, so long as it does not appear the same or any substantial part had been previously patented or described in any printed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision tempers the strictness of the prior-use defence where the patentee acted in good faith and the alleged prior use was foreign and not in printed publication or patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion to award costs when claim is overbroad but some new part was truly infringed
rubrics_metrics.description: When plaintiff fails because his specification or claim embraces more than that of which he was the first inventor, 'if it shall appear that the defendant had used or violated any part of the invention justly and truly specified and claimed as new, it shall be in the power of the court to adjudge and award, as to costs, as may appear to be just and equitable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if plaintiff's overall claim fails, courts may award costs or equitable relief where defendant has infringed genuinely new, truly specified parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer for inadvertent over-claiming (§7, act of 1837)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who 'through inadvertence, accident, or mistake' has made his specification or claim too broad may make a written disclaimer of such parts, attested and recorded in the Patent Office on payment (e.g., $10), and such disclaimer shall thenceforth be taken as part of the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimer preserves the remainder of the patentee's rights (any material and substantial part truly his own) and must be recorded; it does not affect pending actions except as to questions of unreasonable neglect or delay in filing the disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: No examination of prior-use witnesses without prior notice
rubrics_metrics.description: No witness can be examined to prove a prior use of the invention unless notice of his name and residence has been given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical enforcement of the statutory notice requirement designed to avoid surprise and allow plaintiff to investigate prior-use witnesses.
